newsitem.title: GAMBIA: Gambia votes for president,confusion over handover.
newsitem.headline: Gambia votes for president,confusion over handover.

text.p: The people of Gambia voted peacefully in civilian-rule elections on Thursday but experts and diplomats said they feared trouble should the military president lose.
Diplomats said heavy turnout in the capital Banjul meant polling in the interior, where the opposition is strongest, could be even more massive.
This had made the race between military head of state Yahya Jammeh and his toughest civilian challenger, lawyer Ousainou Darboe, too close to call, they said. A winner needs only a simple majority.
But diplomats said the lack of a clear legal provision as to when the winner is sworn in could create a constitutional crisis if Darboe beats Jammeh.

The new constitution, adopted by Jammeh's AFPRC ruling military council after a referendum last month, does not come into force until it is approved by parliament, which will not be in place before December after general elections.

The military council remains in power until the new constitution comes into force -- which will not happen before December after parliamentary elections -- and there is no legal provision anywhere as to when the elected president is sworn in.

"If Jammeh wins then there is no problem as he will just continue in office," said the expert who asked not to be named. "But there could be a problem if Darboe wins and expects to be sworn in tomorrow. His supporters may not understand this."
The Commonwealth and the United Nations described the electoral law and constitutional arrangements as too flawed and called off plans to send observers for the poll.
"The transition is so awkwardly designed that it leaves complete control in the hands of the AFPRC," a Western diplomat said, adding: "This is a recipe for a particularly unstable situation."
Electoral commission chairman Gabriel Roberts aknowledged the legal problem but said it was not for him to decide.

"I don't care about that. That is a problem for the attorney-general," he said. "We are mandated to conduct the elections. We'll conduct the elections, announce the results and handover the results." Roberts said he expected the final
turnout to be bigger than the 87 percent recorded in the. He said there were no reports of major problems. Logistics flaws like missing names on voter lists were being dealt with on the spot.
Polling started started at 7.00 a.m. (0700 GMT) and was scheduled to close at 6.00 p.m. Just over 444,000 people are registered to vote in a population of one million.
First results were due in on Thursday night and Roberts said a winner could be known by late Friday.
Jammeh toppled an elected government in a 1994 coup but international pressure forced him to speed up a transition to democracy, resigning from the army last month to seek election.

The other presidential contenders are Sidia Jatta of the small People's Democratic Organisation for Independence and Socialism, who stood against Jawara in 1992, and hotel manager Amath Bah of the National Reconciliation Party (NRP). Neither is expected to make a serious impact on the election.
The runup to election day has been marked by violent clashes between supporters of the two main rivals.
